title: Self-harm and suicide risk (adult)
subject: psychiatry
summary: Treat the injury or poisoning and start a psychosocial assessment at the same time; do not use risk scales or low, medium or high labels to predict suicide or decide discharge; agree a needs-based plan and written safety plan, restrict access to means, and arrange aftercare within 48 hours if concerns remain.

sections.title: In the emergency department
items: Treat the injury or poisoning without delay (see Acute poisoning: general approach (adult) and specific poisoning protocols). In any overdose, check a paracetamol level because early features may be absent.
At triage establish: severity of injury and urgency, emotional state and distress, immediate safety concerns, safeguarding issues, and willingness to accept medical and mental health care.
Ask what means were used and whether the person still has access to them (tablets, pesticides, weapons, ligatures); discuss removing them collaboratively.
Provide a safe waiting area close to staff; remove items that could be used for self-harm; use trained staff for observation. Do not use mechanical restraint to stop someone leaving.
Assess capacity to refuse treatment. If the person lacks capacity or wants to leave while at serious risk, seek senior advice and act under the relevant mental health or capacity law.
Treat the person with compassion and respect. Do not use punitive or aversive approaches for frequent attenders.

sections.title: Psychosocial assessment
items: A mental health professional should carry out a psychosocial assessment at the earliest opportunity after every episode; do not delay it until medical treatment is finished or use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it.
Explore the reasons for and functions of the self-harm, the degree of suicidal intent (planning, precautions against discovery, belief it would be lethal) and current thoughts or plans.

Identify historic factors (previous self-harm, abuse), changeable factors (mental illness, alcohol or drugs, pain, relationships, debt, housing, work), upcoming events, and protective factors (family, children, reasons for living).
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts; asking does not increase risk.
Older adults: higher suicide rates after self-harm; look for depression, cognitive impairment, physical illness, frailty and loneliness.
Primary care: refer urgently to mental health services if distress is rising, high or sustained, self-harm or suicidal intent is increasing, or you are concerned.

sections.title: Risk formulation, not risk scores (NICE NG225)
items: Do not use risk assessment tools or scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or who is discharged.
Do not use global low, medium or high risk labels for these purposes.
Mental health professionals should make a risk formulation in every psychosocial assessment: needs, current dangers, what could change them and how to keep the person safe.

Consider general hospital admission when safety cannot be assured (for example risk of violence or exploitation), safeguarding planning is incomplete, or the person cannot engage because of distress or intoxication; psychiatric admission when clinically indicated.

sections.title: Safety planning and treatment
items: Develop a written safety plan with the person: triggers and warning signs, own coping strategies, people and places for distraction, family or friends who can help, professional and crisis contacts (including out of hours), and making the environment safe.
Means restriction: agree removal or locked storage of medicines, pesticides, weapons and ligature points, involving family with consent.
Offer a structured CBT-informed psychological intervention tailored to self-harm (for example CBT or problem-solving therapy), typically 4 to 10 sessions, starting as soon as possible.
Treat coexisting depression, anxiety, alcohol or drug misuse, psychosis or personality disorder according to their guidelines. Do not offer drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm.
Do not withhold psychological help because of diagnosis, age, substance misuse or repeated episodes.

sections.title: Discharge and aftercare
items: Before discharge from hospital: psychosocial assessment completed, a management plan agreed with the person and relevant agencies, and aftercare arranged with clear written communication to primary care.
If safety concerns remain, provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.
Give the person a copy of the care plan, safety plan and crisis contact details.
Frequent self-harm or treatment not working: arrange a multidisciplinary review and a named care coordinator.

sections.title: Safer prescribing
items: When prescribing for someone who has self-harmed or may do so, consider overdose toxicity (for example opioids and tricyclic antidepressants), alcohol and drug use, and access to medicines prescribed for others.
Limit quantities (for example weekly prescriptions) by shared decision, ask for unwanted medicines to be returned, and review all medicines after an episode.
Use consultations and medicine reviews to ask about thoughts of self-harm and access to means.

sections.title: India
items: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 115) presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and directs that they receive care and rehabilitation rather than punishment. Medico-legal formalities must not delay treatment.

Pesticide ingestion (organophosphates, aluminium phosphide) is a leading method: advise locked storage of pesticides at home and see Organophosphate and carbamate poisoning and Aluminium phosphide (celphos) poisoning.
Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416) provides free 24-hour mental health support.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Discharging on the basis of a risk score or a low risk label without a psychosocial assessment.
Delaying assessment until the person is sober or medically fit.
Missing paracetamol co-ingestion in an overdose.
Judgemental or punitive care, which reduces future help-seeking.
Prescribing a month's supply of a tricyclic antidepressant or opioid after an overdose.
